statement: How long a drug can still be found by a test after it was last taken is known only roughly. In two narrative reviews, the usual detection times are second-hand figures from single small studies, or from textbooks and laboratory web pages, and the one primary study read that watched people stop (cannabis) could not see when many of them would have turned negative. The first review (Verstraete, 2004, a single-author summary with no stated search) puts one 'typical' study in each cell of its tables for blood, urine and oral fluid, mostly a single controlled dose given to volunteers, in many studies at doses the author calls low compared with street doses and in some to only one or two people, measured as far as possible down to the method's limit of detection rather than at screening cutoffs (some rows use cutoffs), and for several drugs takes the longest times from people who stopped heavy use in prison or on a detoxification ward. From these it summarizes that after a single dose most drugs could be detected in urine for 1.5 to 4 days, in blood for 1 or 2 days and in oral fluid for 5 to 48 hours, and after chronic use in urine for about a week after last use, longer in extreme cases (benzoylecgonine, a breakdown product of cocaine, 22 days after last use in people using cocaine heavily; cannabis up to about 3 months, the longest reports, 93 and 95 days, being called probably exceptional); hair holds drugs longest, depending on its length, with few data on single doses. It calls detection times extremely variable: they depend on the amount, the route, acute or chronic use, the fluid tested, the test's limit or cutoff, the substance sought and differences between people. In one study it cites, urine was last positive after a single controlled dose of methamphetamine at 87 hours on average (46 to 144) at the method's limit of quantification but at 43 hours (22 to 65) at cutoffs of 500 ng/mL methamphetamine and 200 ng/mL amphetamine. After heavy use, times ran longer than the single-dose figures: in a series of 63 men described as dependent on heroin, 88.4% still screened positive for morphine after 1 day and 44.8% after 6 days (the review gives neither the numbers tested each day nor when the days start), and in 18 people housed on a closed research unit, the last positive cocaine screen came on average 81 hours (34 to 162) after the last use they reported. The second review (Moeller et al., 2017, a clinical review for clinicians) gives a table of 'approximate' urine detection times, adapted from the authors' 2008 review, with no cutoff, test, amount or conditions for any value (for example cocaine metabolites 2 to 4 days; heroin, as morphine, 48 hours; amphetamine and methamphetamine 48 hours; diazepam 30 days and lorazepam 3 days; cannabis 3 days after a single use, 5 to 7 days with use 4 times a week, 10 to 15 days with daily use and more than 30 days in a chronic heavy smoker); its nine sources are a 1987 report, a pain-medicine review, a textbook, the 2008 review, two laboratory web pages, a psychiatry textbook chapter, the 2004 review and a pharmacists' newsletter. It adds that a result below the cutoff is reported as negative, which means the level was below the cutoff, not that the drug was absent, and that the heroin-specific breakdown product 6-acetylmorphine shows in urine only up to about 8 hours. In the one primary study read (Goodwin et al., 2008), 60 adults in the USA who reported cannabis dependence or abuse and regular smoking (on average 9.4 joints a week on 10.6 of the last 14 days) lived on a closed research unit under 24-hour medical surveillance with random drug tests for up to 30 days, and every urine sample was screened by immunoassay at the US federal workplace cutoff of 50 ng/mL; days since last use before admission were not reported, so every time runs from admission. The last positive screen came 0 to 29.8 days after admission, on average 4.6, 9.7 and 15.4 days in the groups whose first sample held the least, middling and most THCCOOH, the breakdown product tested for (relative to creatinine: up to 50, 51 to 150 and above 150 ng/mg; 19, 21 and 20 people). These averages are minimums: 13 of the 20 in the highest group were still screening positive on their last day of observation (on average day 19; for 4 of them day 30), and of the 16 people watched for 27 days or more, 6, all in the highest group, were still positive when watching ended (editors' count from Table II). Six of the 60 never screened positive on the unit, and in 43 of the 46 people who had both negative and positive screens a positive came after the first negative (editors' count), the pattern of positive, negative and positive again that the authors describe as levels fall. None of these sources gives the detection time for a particular person, amount or test. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: How long do drugs show up on a drug test? It is known only roughly. Two expert reviews, which are not new studies, give the usual figures. One sums up that after one use, most drugs showed in urine for about 1.5 to 4 days, in blood for 1 to 2 days and in saliva for up to 2 days, and for longer after heavy use. But each figure comes from one small study, some of only one or two people given a single dose in a lab, or from textbooks and lab websites, and the result depends on the test: in one study, a dose of meth was found in urine for about 87 hours at a lab's lowest limit but 43 hours at a higher cutoff. After heavy use, figures ran longer: among 63 men described as dependent on heroin, 45 in 100 still tested positive for morphine after 6 days. In the one study that watched people stop, 60 regular cannabis smokers lived on a locked research ward for up to 30 days, counted from when they arrived, not from their last use. Their last positive came anywhere from day 0 to day 30; 13 of the 20 with the highest levels were still positive when watching ended, so the study's averages of about 5 to 15 days undercount, and positives often came back after a negative. A negative result only means the level was below the test's cutoff.
population: People tested for drugs after use: in the studies summarized second-hand by two narrative reviews, mostly healthy volunteers given a single controlled dose (some studies of one or two people) and people who stopped regular use in prison, on a detoxification ward or on a closed research unit; in the one primary study read, 60 adults aged 18 to 45 in the USA (46 men, 14 women; 50 African American; mean age 26.9) who reported cannabis dependence or abuse (DSM-IV terms) and smoking on average 9.4 joints a week on 10.6 of the last 14 days, kept abstinent on a closed research unit
exposure: Last use of a drug, as a single controlled dose given by researchers or as the end of regular use (in prison, on a detoxification ward or on admission to a closed research unit), followed by tests of urine, blood, oral fluid or hair; in the primary study, cannabis smoked before admission (amounts and THC content unknown; days since last use not reported), then enforced abstinence for up to 30 days
comparator: None: detection times are described, not compared with a control group; in some reviewed studies the same samples were read at different limits or cutoffs; in the primary study, groups formed by the THCCOOH/creatinine of the first urine sample
outcome: Detection time: how long after a single dose, after last reported use or after admission a drug or its breakdown product was found above the stated detection limit or cutoff; in the primary study, days from admission to the first negative and to the last positive urine screen at 50 ng/mL, and whether people were still screening positive when observation ended
magnitude: Verstraete (2004), as summarized (pp. 200, 204): single dose, urine 1.5–4 days, blood 1–2 days, oral fluid 5–48 hours (low ng/mL level); chronic use, urine about 1 week after last use; extreme cases cocaine 22 days, cannabis up to 3 months (longest reports 93 and 95 days, called probably exceptional). Methamphetamine after one controlled dose, last detection: 87.2 ± 51 h (46–144) at 2.5 ng/mL; 51.6 ± 26.3 h (25–77) at 250 and 100 ng/mL; 42.7 ± 22.8 h (22–65) at 500 and 200 ng/mL (methamphetamine and amphetamine). Heroin: 63 men, morphine by immunoassay positive in 88.4%, 74.2%, 64.2%, 57.1%, 63.3% and 44.8% after 1 to 6 days (numbers per day not given); detoxification ward (52 people), total morphine (LOD 25 ng/mL) 4.95 days on average, at most 11.3; 6-acetylmorphine 5 h on average, at most 34.5 h. Cocaine: 18 people on a closed unit, immunoassay cutoff 300 ng/mL, last positive 57.5 ± 31.6 h (11–147) after admission and 81 ± 34 h (34–162) after last reported use. Cannabis, detoxification ward: urine THCCOOH (LOD 10 ng/mL) 4.9 days on average, at most 18. Moeller et al. (2017), Table 2 ('approximate'; no cutoff, test, amount or conditions): alcohol 7–12 h; amphetamine 48 h; methamphetamine 48 h; barbiturates short-acting 24 h, long-acting 3 weeks; benzodiazepines short-acting (lorazepam) 3 days, long-acting (diazepam) 30 days; cocaine metabolites 2–4 days; marijuana single use 3 days, 4 times a week 5–7 days, daily 10–15 days, chronic heavy smoker more than 30 days; codeine 48 h; heroin (morphine) 48 h; hydromorphone 2–4 days; methadone 3 days; morphine 48–72 h; oxycodone 2–4 days; phencyclidine 8 days; synthetic cannabinoids single use 72 h, chronic more than 72 h; synthetic cathinones variable. Text: cannabis more than 30 days after stopping in chronic use, up to 72 h after a single exposure in people who do not use it; 6-acetylmorphine up to 8 h; ethyl glucuronide (alcohol) 2–5 days. Goodwin et al. (2008), 60 people, screen 50 ng/mL, days from admission, mean ± SD by first-sample THCCOOH/creatinine 0–50 (n = 19), 51–150 (n = 21) and above 150 ng/mg (n = 20): first negative 0.6 ± 0.8, 3.2 ± 2.8, 4.7 ± 4.8; last positive 4.6 ± 5.6 (abstract 4.3; 4.55 from the 13 individual values, editors' calculation), 9.7 ± 6.4, 15.4 ± 9.8; ranges 0.0–16.1 (first negative) and 0.0–29.8 (last positive). Still positive on the last day of observation: 13 of 20 in the highest group (mean last day 19; 4 on day 30); by the editors' count with the rule that reproduces these figures, 4 of 19 and 5 of 21 in the other groups (the Discussion says 2 in the lowest), 22 of the 54 who ever screened positive. Observed 27 days or more: 16, of whom 6 still positive at the end (last positives 27.3–29.8 days). Never positive on the unit: 6 of 60. A positive after the first negative: 43 of the 46 with both (42 of 45 without the impossible row F) (editors' counts from Table II).

evidence.extracted: Single-author review published under the heading 'Basel Proceedings', by an author from the Clinical Biology Laboratory of Ghent University Hospital, with no stated search, selection criteria or appraisal. Data on detection times come from controlled administration to volunteers, in many studies at doses the author calls relatively low compared with street doses, or from people forced to stop (often chronic) use, for example on imprisonment or detoxification, which gives no information on the detection time after a single dose. In Tables 1 to 3 (blood, urine, oral fluid) the times are based as much as possible on the methods' limits of quantification or detection rather than on cutoffs. Detection time depends on the dose, the preparation and route, acute or chronic use, the fluid analysed, the detection limit or cutoff, the molecule or metabolite sought, the pH and concentration of urine or oral fluid, and individual differences in metabolism (and, in the abstract, renal clearance).

evidence.extracted: Cutoffs define the concentrations needed for a positive result; a result below the cutoff is reported as negative, which means the concentration was lower than the cutoff, not that the substance was absent. Laboratories may use cutoffs that differ from the federal ones, which were set for adults in the workplace; lower cutoffs reduce false negatives but may increase false positives. Federal workplace cutoffs (Table 1), screen then confirmation (ng/mL): marijuana metabolites 50, then THCCOOH 15; cocaine metabolites 150, then benzoylecgonine 100; codeine/morphine 2000 and 2000; 6-acetylmorphine 10 and 10; phencyclidine 25 and 25; amphetamine/methamphetamine 500, then 250 each; MDMA 500, then MDMA, MDA and MDEA 250 each.

evidence.extracted: Reporting problems: the abstract gives 4.3 days as the lowest group's mean time to the last positive, against 4.6 in Table II and the Discussion; row F is impossible (last positive at 3.1 days, after observation ended at 2.2 days); the Results say all specimens in the 0–50 group screened negative by eight days after the first negative, but participant LL was positive at 21.8 days; the Discussion says 2 participants in the lowest group were positive on their last day; the abstract and Conclusions offer the group means as guidelines for interpreting tests, and the Conclusions expect detection rates of 60 to 100% for 28 days after the first negative in the highest group, without saying that many participants were still positive when observation ended. No funding or conflict-of-interest statement is printed; all authors were NIDA staff and the study ran on NIDA's own unit. Editors' sum: the abstract's 6,158 specimens against 5,916 in Table II.

risk_of_bias.note: The reviews' figures cannot be appraised: one author chose one study per cell with no stated search (card sc_verstraete_2004: high), and the clinical review's table comes from textbooks, laboratory web pages, a newsletter and older reviews (card sc_moeller_2017: high). In the primary study (card sc_goodwin_2008: JBI moderate), times run from admission rather than last use, and the last positive is cut off by the end of observation in 22 of the 54 people who ever screened positive; the statement words the averages as minimums, but the true times cannot be recovered, and the paper has internal inconsistencies (an impossible row; 4.3 against 4.6 days; a lowest group said to be all negative by eight days that includes one person positive at 21.8 days).

inconsistency.note: Figures differ widely between studies, drugs, fluids and cutoffs, but the differences follow the conditions the statement gives (single dose against heavy use, detection limit against cutoff, length of follow-up), and the direction agrees: days after a single dose, longer after heavy use, longest for cannabis.

indirectness.note: The question is how long drugs show on the tests people meet. The typical figures come from single, often low, controlled doses in a few volunteers, measured at laboratory detection limits (which give longer times than a screening cutoff, as the methamphetamine example shows) or at assorted cutoffs, and the clinical review's values carry no conditions at all. The primary study used one screening cutoff (50 ng/mL), counted from admission, and studied one selected US sample (77% men, 83% African American, paid, reporting dependence or abuse).

imprecision.note: Each table entry rests on one study, some of one or two people; the heroin percentages come without the numbers tested each day; in the primary study only 16 people were watched for 27 days or more, so the late part of the picture rests on few people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for narrative reviews or a single case series.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: In the primary study, later last positives went with higher first-sample levels, but the groups were formed by that level and the fits are lines through three group means; not used.

grade.reasoning: Detection times are rated as descriptions (METHODS §6.3): the controlled-dose studies behind the reviews have no comparison group, and the primary study is a case series; start low. Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 (see the domain notes) take it to very low, the floor. The figures from the two narrative reviews are second-hand and the statement says so; the 2004 review reports the numbers of the primary studies it summarizes, which is the only way they are seen here. The one primary study read (Goodwin et al., 2008) is the strongest evidence for cannabis because abstinence was enforced, so later positive screens reflect what was left in the body, not new use; but it cannot give detection times from last use, and its averages are minimums. Status replicated: the direction (days after a single dose; longer, up to weeks, after heavy regular use, most of all for cannabis) agrees across separate studies described in the reviews (for cannabis, single-cigarette studies and a detoxification ward of 52 people) and the primary study; but every specific figure rests on one study, and only one primary study was read. Nothing is phrased as advice on avoiding or passing a test; the clinical review's section on tampering with samples was not used.

(2001, detoxification ward; Forensic Sci Int 119, 248–253), Narongchai et al. (2002, 63 men; J Med Assoc Thai 85, 82–86), Preston et al. (2002, cocaine on a closed unit; J Anal Toxicol 26, 393–400), the authors' own earlier reviews (Vandevenne, Vandenbussche & Verstraete, 2000; Moeller, Lee & Kissack, 2008, Mayo Clin Proc 83, 66–76) and Lowe et al. (2009); neither review prints DOIs. Editors' counts from Goodwin's Table II: data/verification/pdf-2026-11-26/763_counts.py. Not covered here, though the 2017 review describes it: screens that miss a drug altogether (opiate screens and fentanyl, methadone, buprenorphine or oxycodone; benzodiazepine screens and lorazepam, alprazolam or clonazepam; cannabis screens and synthetic cannabinoids).
